definitions.text: A kind of close carriage with two or four wheels, usually a public vehicle. "A cab came clattering up." Thackeray. door behind; or one seat parallel to the driver's, with the entrance from the side or front. Hansom cab. See Hansom.
The covered part of a locomotive, in which the engineer has his station. Knight.
A Hebrew dry measure, containing a little over two (2.37) pints. W. H. Ward. 2 Kings vi. 25.
Tradition; occult doctrine. See Cabala [Obs.] Hakewill.
A secret. [Obs.] "The measuring of the temple, a cabal found out but lately." B. Jonson.

A number of persons united in some close design, usually to promote their private views and interests in church or state by intrigue; a secret association composed of a few designing persons; a junto. cabinet consisted of five persons, the initial letters of whose names made up the word cabal; Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley, and Lauderdale. Macaulay.

The secret artifices or machinations of a few persons united in a close design; in intrigue. By cursed cabals of women. Dryden. considered to be bad is the idea common to these terms. A combination is an organized union of individuals for mutual support, in urging their demands or resisting the claims of others, and may be good or bad according to circumstances; as, a combiniation of workmen or of employers to effect or to prevent a chang in prices. A cabal is a secret association of a few individuals who seek by cunning practices to obtain office and power. A faction is a larger body than a cabal, employed for selfish purposes in agitating the community and working up an excitement with a view to change the existing order of things. "Selfishness, insubordination, and laxity of morals give rise to combinations, which belong particularly to the lower orders of society. Restless, jealous, ambitious, and little minds are ever forming cabals. Factions belong especially to free governments, and are raised by busy and turbulent spirits for selfish porposes". Crabb.
To unite in a small party to promote private views and interests by intrigue; to intrigue; to plot. Caballing still against it with the great. Dryden.

A kind of occult theosophy or traditional interpretation of the Scriptures among Jewish rabbis and certain mediæval Christians, which treats of the nature of god and the mystery of human existence. It assumed that every letter, word, number, and accent of Scripture contains a hidden sense; and it teaches the methods of interpretation for ascertaining these occult meanings. The cabalists pretend even to foretell events by this means.
Secret science in general; mystic art; mystery.
The secret science of the cabalists.
A superstitious devotion to the mysteries of the religion which one professes. [R] Emerson.
One versed in the cabala, or the mysteries of Jewish traditions. "Studious cabalists." Swift.
In a cabalistic manner.
Of or pertaining to the cabala; containing or conveying an occult meaning; mystic. The Heptarchus is a cabalistic of the first chapter of Genesis. Hallam.
To use cabalistic language. [R] Dr. H. More.
One who cabals. A close caballer and tongue-valiant lord. Dryden.

An ancient Spanish land tenure similar to the English knight's fee; hence, in Spain and countries settled by the Spanish, a land measure of varying size. In Cuba it is about 33 acres; in Porto Rico, about 194 acres; in the Southwestern United States, about 108 acres.
A knight or cavalier; hence, a gentleman.
Of or pertaining to a horse.

Caballine aloes. Caballine aloes, an inferior and impure kind of aloes formerly used in veterinary practice; -- called also horse aloes. - fabled to have been formed by a stroke from the foot of the winged horse Pegasus.
A horse. [Sp. Amer.]
A tavern; a house where liquors are retailed. [Obs. as an English word.]
A flat basket or frail for figs, etc.; Hence, a lady's flat workbasket, reticule, or hand bag; -- often written caba. C. Bronté.
A speciec of armadillo of the genus Xenurus (X. unicinctus and X. hispidus); the tatouay. [Written also Kabassou.]

An esculent vegetable of many varieties, derived from the wild Brassica oleracea of Europe. The common cabbage has a compact head of leaves. The cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, etc., are sometimes classed as cabbages.
The terminal bud of certain palm trees, used, like, cabbage, for food. See Cabbage tree, below.

The cabbage palmetto. See below. Cabbage aphis (Zoöl.), a green plant-louse (Aphis brassicæ) which lives upon the leaves of the cabbage. vittata) which lives, in the larval state, on the roots, and when adult, on the leaves, of cabbage and other cruciferous plants. Europe and America, and the Allied P. oleracea, a native American species) which, in the larval state, devours the leaves of the cabbage and the turnip. See Cabbage worm, below. which feeds, in the larval or maggot state, on the roots of the cabbage, often doing much damage to the crop. silly person; a numskull. along the coast from North Carolina to Florida. large and heavy blossoms. terminal bud called a cabbage, as the Sabal Palmetto of the United States, and the Euterpe oleracea and Oreodoxa oleracea of the West Indies. butterfies, which attacks cabbages. The most common is usully the larva of a white butterfly. See Cabbage Butterfly, above. The cabbage cutworms, which eat off the stalks or young plants during the night, are the larvæ of several species of moths, of the genus Agrotis. See Cutworm. oleracea), from which the cabbage, cauliflower, , broccoli, etc., have been derived by cultivation.
To form a head like that the cabbage; as, to make lettuce cabbage. Johnson.
To purloin or embezzle, as the pieces of cloth remaining after cutting out a garment; to pilfer. Your tailor . . . cabbages whole yards of cloth. Arbuthnot.
Cloth or clippings cabbaged or purloined by one who cuts out garments.
One who works at cabbling.
The process of breaking up the flat masses into which wrought iron is first hammered, in order that the pieces may be reheated and wrought into bar iron.
The finest kind of silk received from India.
A pole or beam used in Scottish games for tossing as a trial of strength.
A California fish (Hemilepidotus spinosus), allied to the sculpin.
The capybara. See Capybara.
A cottage or small house; a hut. Swift. A hunting cabin in the west. E. Everett.
A small room; an inclosed place. So long in secret cabin there he held Her captive. Spenser.
A room in ship for officers or passengers. Cabin boy, a boy whose duty is wait on the officers and passengers in the cabin of a ship.
To live in, or as in, a cabin; to lodge. I'll make you . . . cabin in a cave. Shak.
To confine in, or as in, a cabin. I am cabined, cribbed, confined, bound in To saucy doubts and fears. Shak.
A hut; a cottage; a small house. [Obs.] Hearken a while from thy green cabinet, The rural song of careful Colinet. Spenser.
A small room, or retired apartment; a closet.
A private room in which consultations are held. Philip passed some hours every day in his father's cabinet. Prescott.

The advisory council of the chief executive officer of a nation; a cabinet council. privy coucilors who actually transact the immediate business of the government. Mozley & W. executive departments of the government, namely, the Secretary of State, of the Treasury, of War, of the Navy, of the Interior, and of Agiculture, the Postmaster-general ,and the Attorney-general. 5. (a) A set of drawers or a cupboard intended to contain articles of value. Hence: (b) A decorative piece of furniture, whether open like an étagère or closed with doors. See Etagere.
Any building or room set apart for the safe keeping and exhibition
Suitable for a cabinet; small. He [Varnhagen von Ense] is a walking cabinet edition of Goethe. For. Quar. Rev.
To inclose [R.] Hewyt.
One whose occupation is to make cabinets or other choice articles of household furniture, as tables, bedsteads, bureaus, etc.
The art or occupation of making the finer articles of household furniture.
The art or occupation of working upon wooden furniture requiring nice workmanship; also, such furniture.
,n.One of the Cabiri.
Certain deities originally worshiped with mystical rites by the Pelasgians in Lemnos and Samothrace and afterwards throughout Greece; art of working metals. [Written also Cabeiri.] Liddell & Scott.
Same as Cabiric.
Of or pertaining to the Cabiri, or to their mystical worship. [Written also Cabiritic.]
A large, strong rope or chain, of considerable length, used to retain a vessel at anchor, and for other purposes. It is made of hemp, of steel wire, or of iron links.
A rope of steel wire, or copper wire, usually covered with some protecting, or insulating substance; as, the cable of a suspension bridge; a telegraphic cable.
(Arch)

A molding, shaft of a column, or any other member of convex, rounded section, made to resemble the spiral twist of a rope; -- called also cable molding. Bower cable, the cable belonging to the bower anchor. continuously running endless rope operated by a stationary motor. merchant service vary in length from 100 to 140 fathoms or more; but as a maritime measure, a cable's length is either 120 fathoms (720 feet), or about 100 fathoms (600 feet, an approximation to one tenth of a nautical mile). stowed. (b) A coil of a cable. moor a ship in a place sheltered from wind and heavy seas. it may run out of the ship; to let more cable run out of the hawse hole. prevent its being, worn or galled in the hawse, et. out and go overboard, as when there is not time to weigh anchor. Hence, in sailor's use, to die.
To fasten with a cable.
(Arch.)
To ornament with cabling. See Cabling.
To telegraph by a submarine cable [Recent]
Fastened with, or attached to, a cable or rope. "The cabled stone." Dyer.
(Arch.)
Adorned with cabling.
A message sent by a submarine telegraphic cable.
(Naut.)
Composed of three three-stranded ropes, or hawsers, twisted together to form a cable.
Twisted after the manner of a cable; as, a cable-laid gold chain. Simmonds.
A little cable less than ten inches in circumference.

The decoration of a fluted shaft of a column or of a pilaster with reeds, or rounded moldings, which seem to be laid in the hollows of the fluting. These are limited in length to about one third of the height of the shaft.
The driver of a cab.
A small piece of mutton or other meat roasted on a skewer; -- so called in Turkey and Persia.
A leg of mutton roasted, stuffed with white herrings and sweet herbs. Wright.
To roast, as a cabob. Sir. T. Herbert.
Showing the full face, but nothing of the neck; -- said of the head of a beast in armorial bearing. [Written also caboshed.]
A stone of convex form, highly polished, but not faceted; also, the style of cutting itself. Such stones are said to be cut en cabochon.
The whole collection; the entire quantity or number; -- usually in the phrase the whole caboodle. [Slang, U.S.] Bartlett.
(Naut.)
A house on deck, where the cooking is done; -- commonly called the galley.
(Railroad)
A car used on freight or construction trains for brakemen, workmen, etc.; a tool car. [U. S.]
Navigation along the coast; the details of coast pilotage.
The pronghorn antelope. [Also written cabrit, cabret.]
An apple-green mineral, a hydrous arseniate of nickel, cobalt, and magnesia; -- so named from the Sierra Cabrera, Spain.

A name applied to various species of edible fishes of the genus Serranus, and related genera, inhabiting the Meditarranean, the coast of California, etc. In California, some of them are also called rock bass and kelp salmon.
A curvet; a leap. See Capriole. The cabrioles which his charger exhibited. Sir W. Scott.
A one-horse carriage with two seats and a calash top.
Same as Cabrée.
A small line made of spun yarn, to bind or worm cables, seize tackles, etc.
